title: Hello_World:_How_to_be_Human_in_the_Age_of_the_Machine
summary:
Hello World: How to Be Human in the Age of the Machine (also titled Hello World: Being Human in the Age of Algorithms) is a book on the growing influence of algorithms and artificial intelligence on human life, authored by mathematician and science communicator Hannah Fry. Fry is an Associate Professor in the mathematics of cities at University College London, where she uses mathematical models to study patterns in human behaviour and has worked with governments, police forces, health analysts, and supermarkets.

The book poses questions about who should determine human fate — a human or an algorithm — and welcomes readers to the age of the algorithm, where machines make important decisions in healthcare, transport, finance, security, and criminal justice. Hannah Fry takes readers on a tour of the good, the bad, and the ugly of the algorithms that surround us, lifting the lid on their inner workings, demonstrating their power, exposing their limitations, and examining whether they really are an improvement on the humans they are replacing.

The book covers topics including the development of sophisticated data engineering, the role of data brokers, Cambridge Analytica, micro-targeted advertising, and the use of social media to manipulate people's emotions. It also examines machine learning applications including analysis of medical images, self-driving cars, and crime prediction. Additionally, it discusses the potential benefits of employing algorithms to improve consistency in judicial sentencing decisions, whilst recognising the ability of algorithms to perpetuate the inequalities of the past.

The author concludes that it is a "both/and" world rather than "either/or": humans need to accept that algorithms are here to stay, but must also critically examine their assumptions, workings, and answers. The book was praised by The Times as "one of the best books yet written on data and algorithms," and The Guardian noted that "this book illustrates why good science writers are essential."
